messages.subject: ggExtra and gridExtra
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

Let me apologize for this is almost off-topic, but following an
off-line suggestion I renamed the packages ggextra and gridextra to
ggExtra and gridExtra respectively. This is to maintain a consistent
naming scheme following latticeExtra and zooExtra.

I take this opportunity to explain how these two packages relate to ggplot2,

- gridExtra (http://code.google.com/p/gridextra/) provides
experimental grobs ("graphical objects" for Grid graphics), including
so far: tableGrob (display a data.frame), barbedGrob (points and lines
as in type = 'b'). It also provides an arrange() function to
conveniently place ggplot2 objects and grobs on a page (a wrapper
around grid.layout).

- ggExtra (http://code.google.com/p/ggextra/) provides (highly)
experimental geoms and scales for ggplot2. Currently this includes:

scales:
scale_colour_dichromat(),

geoms:
"geom_ellipse" "geom_field" "geom_fielduv" "geom_ngon" "geom_star"

themes:
"theme_bb" "theme_bw2" "theme_dark" "theme_flashy" "theme_gray2"
"theme_minimal" "theme_talk"

Needless to say, participation is very welcome!

baptiste

messages.subject: error message using geom_text with grouped data
messages.subject_clean: error message using geom_text with grouped data
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I'm having problems adding text to a plot. Here's a simplified
reconstruction of what I'm trying to do:

tm<-1:10
v1<-rnorm(10)
v2<-rnorm(10)
v3<-rnorm(10)
dat<-data.frame(tm,v1,v2,v3)

ag<-c(2,5,9)
lbl<-c("A","A","B")
labl<-data.frame(ag,lbl)

dm<-melt(dat, id=1)
p<-ggplot(dm, aes(tm, value, group=variable))
p + geom_line(aes(colour=variable))
last_plot() + geom_text(aes(x=ag, y=-2, label=lbl), data=labl)

This then returns the error message: "Error in eval(expr, envir,
enclos) : object 'variable' not found"

Does anyone know of a better way to do this please? (i.e. one that
works!)
Thanks
Eve

messages.subject: Re: error message using geom_text with grouped data
messages.subject_clean: error message using geom_text with grouped data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The problem you have is that your first line, ggplot(dm, aes(tm,
value, group=variable)), defines some global aesthetic mapping for the
plot. These mappings don't work with the last geom you want to use
(hence it fails to find a "variable").

You have at least three options:

1- move all aes() in the geom,

p<-ggplot(dm)
p + geom_line(aes(tm, value, group=variable, colour=variable))

last_plot() + geom_text(aes(x=ag, y=-2, label=lbl), data=labl)

2- overwrite the mapping for the last geom,

p<-ggplot(dm, aes(tm, value, group=variable))
p + geom_line(aes(colour=variable))

last_plot() + geom_text(aes(x=ag, y=-2, label=lbl, group=NA),  data=labl)

3- use annotate()

p <- ggplot(dm, aes(tm, value, group=variable))
p + geom_line(aes(colour=variable))
last_plot() + annotate(geom="text",x=ag, y=-2, label=lbl)

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Two "stupid" questions: 1. how to make the bars start from the axis in a bar chart? 2. how to change the tick mark labels in a barchart?
messages.subject_clean: Two "stupid" questions: 1. how to make the bars start from the axis in a bar chart? 2. how to change the tick mark labels in a barchart?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, all,

I bought the new ggplot2 book and studied extensively. I think the
ggplot2 is the most promising graphic package in
R because of the grammer underlying it. However, the books makes me
confused sometimes.

First, all the examples, especially those bar charts, the bars started
not from the axis. This is easilly seen when
I changed the theme to the all black-white traditional looks. The fact
that the bars are distanced from the X axis make it looks strange.
Also, I could not change the tick mark labels in a barchart. The breaks
() and labels() functions does not work for me in a barchart.

Code:
temp1<-mo1.tc2.0005$contributions
mo1.rel.inf<-data.frame(temp1)
a1<-ggplot(mo1.rel.inf,aes(var,rel.inf),stat="identity")+geom_bar()
+ylim(0,80)
> mo1.rel.inf
              var              rel.inf
1 Complementarity   70.2882460
2               H             25.7461915
3      Ecosystems     3.5824652
4          Origin             0.3830973
So when I plot this by the following, I got the strange results, in
which the bars are in the order of Complementarity, Ecosystems, H, and
Origin.

So I did the following: a1<-ggplot(mo1.rel.inf,aes(sort
(var,increasing=TRUE),rel.inf),stat="identity")+geom_bar()+ylim(0,80)

This time, the y values are correct according to the data, but the
tick mark labels are not in correct order.
So I tried to change the tick mark labels by hand, but failed.
I solved this by doing the following:

mo1.rel.inf$fvar<-factor(seq(1:4),levels=c(1,2,3,4),labels=c
("Complementarity","H","Ecosystems","Origin"))
a1<-ggplot(mo1.rel.inf,aes(fvar,rel.inf),stat="identity")+geom_bar()
+ylim(0,80)

Thank you million times if anyone here could help me with this.

Dan
Graduate Student
Forestry and environmental sciences
Lakehead University
Ontario, Canada

messages.subject: Re: Repost: Changing Bar Widths for Barcharts with Categorical x-axis Variables
messages.subject_clean: Repost: Changing Bar Widths for Barcharts with Categorical x-axis Variables
messages.body_plain:
After continued trial and error, I discovered that a simple:
+ geom_bar(width=0.5) makes categorical bars that
are 1/2 width, etc.

This is an undocumented feature, as a search of the
page: http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_bar.html for the
word "width" revealed no hits.

It appears that position_stack is used automatically
when x is a categorical variable.

I believe it might be clearer if the documentation for
position_stack mentioned this, or contained an
example that used one of the parameters of
position_stack:
position_stack(width=NULL, height=NULL, ...)

As written, the page only has an example for
binwidth= .  In addition, for a ggplot2 newbie,
the default, within parens after position_stack
is somewhat confusing when the "width"
argument is actually added to  geom_bar(),
not position_stack().

Glad you figured it out.

> This is an undocumented feature, as a search of the
> page: http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_bar.html for the
> word "width" revealed no hits.

It's undocumented because width is a bit of strange creature - it's
sort of an aesthetic, but it isn't transformed by any scale and only
really makes sense in cartesian coordinates.  I'm not completely sure
how to document it.

> It appears that position_stack is used automatically
> when x is a categorical variable.

Position stack is always used with geom_bar (unless otherwise
specified), but it doesn't have any relevance to your problem - the
width there is a red herring, and only exists for compatibility with
the other positions which do actually use it.

Hadley

On Thu, Oct 1, 2009 at 3:04 PM, Bogaso <bogaso.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you so much for this mail However I need one more modification.
> As I asked in this thread "http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/
> browse_thread/thread/59802218cdc4d370", I want to remove the extra
> space at left and right edge. I tried following :
>
> last_plot() + scale_x_date(limits = c(as.Date(dat1[1,1]), as.Date(dat1
> [13,1])), major="3 months", minor = "3 months",  format="%b-%Y")
>
>
> However still there are blank spaces at the both edges. i.e. that line-
> plot does not start from the left edge and stop at the right edge. I
> also tried with coord_cartesian(), however it is not working in
> present case. It seems that it does not work with date-class. Can
> anyone please help me how to do that?

First of all, I'd strongly discourage you from doing that, those gaps
have an important perceptual purpose: separating the data from the
axes.  If you remove them you are at substantial risk of confusing the
two.

If you really want to do it, you can do it with this hack:

library(zoo)
dat <- zooreg(rnorm(13), start=as.yearmon("2009-01-01"),
frequency=12)
dat1 <- data.frame(index = index(dat), coredata = coredata(dat))

ggplot(dat1) + geom_line(aes(as.Date(index), coredata))

dt <- scale_x_date(major="3 months", minor = "3 months", format="%b-%Y")
dt$.expand <- c(0, 0)

last_plot() + dt

I personally agree with the idea that having the data touch the axes
is a bad idea. However I know some people won't tolerate axes that
don't meet, or extend further than the data (especially when the data
are bound between 0 and 1), or the absence of a thick box frame around
the plot.

A compromise I found was to add horizontal lines (or vertical) with
annotate() at, say, 0 and 1. In your case that would be an horizontal
line at the base of the bars. If not too obtrusive in colour or
thickness, Tufte might not call it junk.

messages.subject: removing geom_text redundancies
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm getting repeated labels (one per each level in variable) where one
would suffice: e.g. qplot( data=m, x=date, y=value, colour=variable,
label=major_event_desc ) + scale_y_continuous(formatter = "comma") +
geom_text( angle=90, size=3, colour='purple' ) +stat_smooth()

For example, with 2 levels of variable, I get 2 lines but also 2
overlapping indications of "independence day" on july 4th...

Is there any way to specify that the label should occur exactly once?

Here is a reproducible example:

data(economics)
m        <- melt(data=economics[, c(1,2,4,5,6)], id.vars=c('date') )
m$idates <- ifelse(m$date=="1987-07-31", "random date of importance",
"")
qplot(data=m, x=date, y=value, colour=variable, geom=c('line','point'),
label=idates )+ geom_text( angle=90, size=4, colour='purple' ) +
stat_smooth()

Notice that the text "random date of importance" is repeated and
superimposed on itself once for each level of "variable" (i.e. pce,
psavert,
uempmed, unemploy ) making it unreadable.  It would be great to have
something that indicates that it should be rendered only if it has
not been
rendered already.

Best regards,
Avram

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I wonder whether it would be possible (desirable?) to define a
widthDetails.ggplot2 method (and heightDetails) so that grid knows the
size of the legend object.

Consider the following case,

 library(ggplot2)
 p <- qplot(data = mtcars, mpg, hp, geom = "point",
     colour = cyl)
 p1 <- p + opts(legend.position = "none")
 p2 <- qplot(data = mtcars, wt, disp, geom = "point",
     colour = cyl) + opts(legend.position = "none")
 legend <- p + opts(keep = "legend_box")

legend <- ggplotGrob(legend)
top <- ggplotGrob(p1)
bottom <- ggplotGrob(p2)

 layout <- grid.layout(nrow = 2, ncol = 1)

gf = grid.frame(name="gf", layout=layout)

grid.place("gf", top, row=1, col=1)
grid.place("gf", bottom, row=2, col=1)
grid.pack("gf", legend, side="right")

The space allocated by grid.pack clearly doesn't understand that only
the legend is to be drawn (in fact, I'm not sure how it infers the
size of a ggplotGrob at all).

All the best,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Best I could come up with is to bin the thickness data outside ggplot2 first:

test$thick2 = with(test,ifelse(thicknessOfLine<20000,1,ifelse(thicknessOfLine<40000,2,3)))

ggplot(data=test, aes(x_axis)) +
geom_line(aes(y = variable,size= thick2 ),colour="seagreen4") +
scale_size(breaks = c(1,2,3),labels = c('0-20000','20000-40000','40000+'))

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You can specify the breaks as well as the size limits,

test<-read.table("scale_continuous_ex.txt", header=T)

ggplot(data=test, aes(x_axis)) +
geom_line(aes(y = variable,size= thicknessOfLine

),colour="seagreen4")+ scale_size(breaks = c(1,2,4)*1e4, to=
c(0.005,5))

However I think that if you want to set the size for each intermediate
interval, then you're effectively considering your variable as
discrete and you probably want to convert it to factor beforehand.

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Scales and space in faceting
messages.body_plain:
Sorry about that, I was referring to the previous example.  Here is a
"hopefully" reproducible example.  I would like to create a "manhattan
plot" for Genome-wide association studies using faceting and taking
advantage of the 'space="free"' option when using qplot.  POS is base
pair position and needs to be on a fixed x scale so that the distance
between points is important (how far up down the chromosome a
particular point is.  Chromosome 1 is the largest and has, for
simplification Positions 0:100.  Chr 3 has position 0:40, Chr4 has
positions 0:10.

I expect space=free to break the faceted graphs at their upper postion
limit. This is not happening.  Both X and Y scales must be fixed for
publication purpuse

> df <- data.frame(
 CHR=rep(1:6,each=3),
 POS=c(0,10,20,10,20,30,10,15,20,0,5,10,30,31,32,41,40,42),
 SCORE=rep(1:3,6))
> df
   CHR POS SCORE
1    1   0     1
2    1  10     2
3    1  20     3
4    2  10     1
5    2  20     2
6    2  30     3
7    3  10     1
8    3  15     2
9    3  20     3
10   4   0     1
11   4   5     2
12   4  10     3
13   5  30     1
14   5  31     2
15   5  32     3
16   6  41     1
17   6  40     2
18   6  42     3
> p <- qplot(POS,SCORE,data=df) + facet_grid(. ~ CHR, scales="fixed", space="free")
> print(p)

Hope this helps,
Quince

messages.subject: Shape fill?
messages.body_plain:
When combining geom_line() with the shape=0 argument (or any other
open shape), the line goes over the open shape (see attached image
below).  Is there a way to bring the geom_shape() layer to the top and
to make it opaque, so the line runs under it?

http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/web/transparentglyphs.png

Here's some sample code: -
myvar=c(1:10)
myd=data.frame(myvar)
ggplot(myd)+
theme_bw()+
opts(panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(), panel.grid.major = theme_blank
())+
geom_line(aes(x=myvar,y=myvar))+
geom_point(aes(x=myvar,y=myvar),size=3, shape=0)

messages.subject: Mapping variables to lightness
messages.body_plain:
Is it possible to map variables to lightness/brightness/luminance with
ggplot2?

Here's a simple example of a dataset this could be useful on:

n=16
x=rnorm(n)
y=rnorm(n)
l=c(3,5,n-8)
time=unlist(lapply(l,seq_len))
z=rep(letters[1:3],l)
d=data.frame(x,y,z,time)
qplot(x,y,colour=z,group=z,size=I(3),geom="path")

This draws three paths of different lengths and colours. If 'x' and y
'is' position and 'time' is time (either absolute or relative), it
would useful to use the lightness to indicate time, where the old
positions fade away. (An alternative is to use 'alpha', but for
various reasons I prefer not too.)

So, is this possible?

There is in fact two useful ways the lightness could be mapped. One
uses an absolute scale, so that time = 1 is lightest and time = 8 is
darkest (which should be the colour the above code now gives us, not
black). Then all of short pink line will be very light. This is the
way 'size=time' works.

The other one is based on a relative scale, e.g., a scale for each
group. Then the start of the pink line will be very light (e.g.
white), and the end will have full colour.

Both alternatives will be useful in different circumstances.

--
Karl Ove Hufthammer

messages.subject_clean: Problem making a boxplot .... odd error
messages.body_plain:
On Oct 7, 10:14 am, Peter Flom <peterflomconsult...@mindspring.com>
wrote:

> p <- ggplot(math1, x = math_1, y = TFC)
> p + geom_boxplot()
>
> yields
>
> error: attempt to apply non-function

I think you mean ggplot(math1, aes(x=math_1, y=TFC)). The aes()
function creates a mapping from the data frame variable to the x or y
dimension of the graph. You get that weird error because it's not a
syntactic (R) error, it's a semantic (ggplot) error. When you say "x =
math_1" outside of an aes() call, you're telling ggplot to use a fixed
value for all x. But there's no scalar called math_1 in the
environment, so you get an error. (Why it wants a function there is
not clear to me, but I haven't dug through that part of the code.)
This makes more sense if you compare something like aes(color=Z),
which maps the factor Z in the data frame to the color of the points/
lines/whatever in the plot, using default colors. Versus just color=Z,
outside the aes() call, which usually doesn't do what you want it to
do, or color="blue" which does what you would expect.

You might also try constructing the ggplot object and then doing
summary(p) to get some basic/incomplete information on what ggplot
thinks it's trying to do...

 -Harlan

aesthetic, but that's not what I need; I wish to set the hue based on

('luminance') aesthetic, so that one line (in my original example) is
pink with various luminance values, one is green with various
luminance values, and one is blue with various luminance values.

just like colour and size and alpha can be.

messages.subject: Re: Creating ab-line for logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
> Also - I have done things like "defactor" my explanatory variables so
> that I get slopes and intercepts - but I still dont get anything like
> the chart I posted. So the questions below remain unanswered.

Why would you want to convert categorical variables into continuous?

Here's how I'd visualise your data and model:

library(ggplot2)
stack.data <- read.csv("stack.csv")
stack.data$version <- factor(stack.data$version)
stack.data$prob <- with(stack.data, fail / (pass+fail+notexe))

model.bin <- glm(cbind(fail,(pass+fail+notexe)) ~ impl + version,
  family = binomial,data = stack.data)

grid <- with(stack.data, expand.grid(
  impl = levels(impl),
  version = levels(version)
))
grid$prob <- predict(model.bin, grid, type = "response")

ggplot(stack.data, aes(version, prob, colour = impl)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(group = impl), data = grid)

If it's not obvious from the plot, your model isn't very good.  Have
you mislabelled impl for version 1?

Hadley

On Oct 8, 2:52 pm, knguyen <nguyen.h.kh...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you for all the response. I am sorry for the confusion.

> counts of a graph. (hence, the histogram of the degree distribution).
>
> An example:
>
> > degree.dist <- sample(1:20, 1000, replace = T) # sample degree distribution
> > qplot(degree(g), geom = 'histogram') + scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10()
>
> the last step is what I need, but I'd like a scatter plot instead of a
> bar chart. Is it possible?
>

Yes, it's possible. First, it's easiest if you use data.frames.
Second, it's easiest to not use qplot as a beginner. Really. Don't
believe Hadley on this one. :)

d <- data.frame(X=degree.dist)
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=X, y=..count..), stat="bin", binwidth=1)

So, geom_point says plot with points, where the x coordinate comes
from the data and the y coordinate is computed by ggplot. In this
case, by the binning algorithm which is used by histograms. It
generates a new variable called ..count.. which you can use directly.
The binwidth thing is a parameter to bin, and just makes the points
line up with the integers...

(The log scales didn't work for me right away, but I'm sure you can
figure that out with some trial and error!)

 -Harlan

messages.subject: Re: scale_x_discrete : drop argument
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Oct 8, 2009 at 10:55 AM, Xavier <cha...@agroparistech.fr> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I'm running R v 2.9.2 and ggplot2 v 0.8.3
>
> d <- data.frame(x=c("a", "b", "c"), y=1:3)
>
> qplot(x, y, data=d[1:2,]) + scale_x_discrete(drop=FALSE)
> qplot(x, y, data=d[1:2,]) + scale_x_discrete(drop=TRUE)
>
> On my computer, the two graphs are identical (and include "c" on the
> axis). Is that reproducible? If yes, is it a bug or is it me not
> understanding what "drop" should do?

I think this is a bug, but I'm not sure how to fix it. The problem is
that there's a semi-complicated interaction with facetting - if scales
are fixed, then you can only drop levels that don't appear in any of
the facets, and if scales are free and you have categorical variables
then you expect extra levels within a facet to be dropped without
having to also say scale_x_discrete(drop = TRUE).

Maybe I should change the default to drop = TRUE and not override your
choice when scales = "free" as I'm currently doing.  The potential
problem with this is that if you are facetting with scales = "fixed"
and some levels don't appear on every facet, then there's a
possibility the factors will get rearranged.

So maybe a better solution would be to drop levels automatically
whenever drop = T OR when scales = "free".

Ok - I've tried this out and it seems to work ok, so it will be fixed
in the next version.

Hadley

--
http://had.co.nz/

I don't think there is a possibility to add a seccond x-axis with
ggplot, but you can define your own axis breaks and labels.

<yourplot> + scale_x_continuous("wt",breaks=c(1.5,3.5),labels=c("Event1","Event2"))

scale_x_continuous. The problem with overlapping labels can also occure
on the x-axis, but maybe choosing different y values with annotate can

you're going to end up reshaping it column-by-column or frame-by-frame, or at least I did.  melt chokes on my data (methylation data mostly, some snps, some expression sets)

ggplot2 doesn't really expect an eSet-derived object to play with.  Although, if you write some hooks so that ggplot2 does play nice with ExpressionSet-like classes, you will be a hero forever.

Anyways, how many peptides do you have?  A ton?  Can you post up some code and a little throwaway eSet-like data file that resembles your own?  I've dealt with this sort of thing in my code, so I am curious how others will approach the same problem.

On Sat, Oct 10, 2009 at 12:56 AM, Dr Proteome <reneh...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear people,
> I'm trying to analyse microarray data and I've started using R only a
> few months ago. So I've been playing around with several packages but
> only recently I found ggplot2 and it looks great and exactly what I
> need to visualise my data and results. Sadly I have not been able to
> try it on my own data yet.
> The problem is this: ( I still feel an R-novice so please forgive me
> if my explanation looks a bit unclear)
>
> My data is organised in a muliset (peptide microarray for protein-
> binding studies) ,
> - the phenoData contains the annotation of the samples that are
> applied to the arrays
> - the featureData contains all the info of the peptides that are on
> the chip (name sequence, concentration, position etc)
> - assayData: for each peptide several parameters are available
> (signal, background, shape etc)
>
> my problem here is, how to get my data in the right format to be able
> to apply ggplot2?
>
> I was looking at the diamonds dataset, annd understand the data
> structure.
> Basically every peptide  on each array I use can be considered as a
> single diamond for which phenoData (ID variables) , featureData and
> assayData  is available.
> I have not been able to reformat my multiset into the format as shown
> in the diamonds table.
>
> I have been using the reshape package to melt the data frame but was
> only partially succesful.
>
> Can you give me some advice on what would be the best way to solve
> this problem (if available)?
>
> thanks for the help!
> Rene
>
>
>

--George Box

messages.subject: geom_pointrange and position argument
messages.body_plain:
Hey,

i want to plot some data with discrete x-axis and continuous y-axis.
For each break on the x-axis, 4 different y values exists.

With position="identity" the points or pointranges overlap each other,
so i tried "dodge" and "jitter".

I don't see any changes with "dodge" and with "jitter" for some points
it's a bit difficult to identify the belonging x-axis breaks.

Any ideas how to move the ponts a little bit to the left and the right
(the best would be a fixed amount for each variable level, see example
below).

I can't use facets, because I use it allready, the example below is just
the data for one facet.

example:

library(ggplot2)
d = structure(list(Bundesland = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("Eisenstadt (BGL)",
"Graz (STM)", "Klagenfurt (KTN)", "Kremsmünster (OOE)", "Salzburg (SBG)",

"CLM_B1", "CLM_A1B", "CLM_B1", "CLM_A1B", "CLM_B1", "CLM_A1B",
"CLM_B1", "Remo_A1B", "Remo_B1", "Remo_A1B", "Remo_B1", "Remo_A1B",
"Remo_B1", "Remo_A1B", "Remo_B1"), Dekade = structure(c(1L, 1L,
2L, 2L, 3L, 3L, 4L, 4L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 3L, 4L, 4L), .Label = c("1961-2000",
"2001-2030", "2031-2070", "2071-2100"), class = "factor"), SRES = structure(c(1L,
2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L), .Label = c("A1B",
"B1"), class = "factor"), mean = c(11.3087444999722, 11.3087444999722,
11.7518043639496, 11.8533944409593, 12.3789610591686, 12.229776183631,
13.1621765239205, 12.7607377942529, 13.0388901869159, 13.0388901869159,
13.610393167902, 13.5922494360296, 14.4502453271028, 14.1906542056075,
15.6681931464174, 15.178800623053), sd = c(0.558445359072224,
0.558445359072224, 0.643855367030372, 0.580734781470385, 0.736930693104638,
0.649717330030318, 0.666825505243008, 0.689166881171515, 0.649813010593805,
0.649813010593805, 0.598086022592438, 0.530013751143853, 0.802553323052953,
0.474180312808992, 0.682137990645673, 0.705061505200587)), .Names = c("Bundesland",
"variable", "Dekade", "SRES", "mean", "sd"
), row.names = c(NA, 16L), class = "data.frame")

ggplot(d) + geom_pointrange(aes(x=Dekade,y=mean,colour=variable,
		  ymin=mean-sd,ymax=mean+sd),position="jitter")

thanks for your help.

  stefan

>> df <- expand.grid(year=seq(1999,2008),
>>         type=c("Commodities", "Intermediate", "Final Products",

>>         dir=c("Imports", "Exports"))

>> df$Value = runif(nrow(df), 5, 30) * ifelse(df$dir=="Imports", -1, 1)

>> p <- ggplot(df, aes(x=year, y=Value, fill=type)) +
>>         geom_bar(stat="identity", data=subset(df, dir=="Imports")) +
>>         geom_bar(stat="identity", data=subset(df, dir=="Exports"))

>> df.m <- melt(df, id=c("type", "year", "dir"))

messages.subject: Re: Mapping variables to lightness
messages.body_plain:
> That makes sense, there is no need to modify other scales as I wrongly
> hypothesized.
>
> As far as I understand though, such a scale would require adding a
> "luminance" parameter to all relevant geoms, right?

No, because the scale would emit the colour aesthetic.  It's a
different situation to alpha, because colour and alpha are
independent, while luminance and hue both contribute to colour.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: does geom_text jitter when using hjust?
messages.subject_clean: does geom_text jitter when using hjust?
messages.body_plain:
The hjust parameter is proportional to the width of the text.  You
probably want something like:

ggplot(dm, aes(variable, value,group=Type,label=Type,size=I.alt))+
 geom_line(aes(col=value2))+
 geom_text(aes(as.numeric(variable) + 0.1), data=subset(dm,
variable=="idx08"),hjust= 0,
   size=3)

Hadley

I just noticed this thread, and I don't think that it's been pointed
out so far, but it appears that you're using a 64-bit version
("x86_64") of R. Which raises two issues:

1. As far as I know, CRAN Mac binaries are 32-bit, which might mean
that you're using an R compiled from source by someone else. Which
might explain some differences. The example works on my 32-bit version
("i386") of R 2.9.2 from CRAN.

2. I wonder if ggplot or anything it depends on has a bug that causes
problems when you compile it 64-bit or link in 64-bit versions of
other libraries.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to create a simple bar plot with error bars, but am having
trouble making the barplots a lighter grey so that the error bars are
more visible.  Here is an example.

Temp<-c("H","L","M")
avg<-c(63.8,47.3,58.6)
sd<-c(2.8,2.7,3.3)
dat.temp<-data.frame(cbind(Temp,as.numeric(as.character
(avg)),as.numeric(as.character(sd))))

rate.plot<-qplot(Temp,avg,data=dat.temp,geom="bar",position="dodge")
dodge <- position_dodge(width=0.9)
rate.plot+geom_linerange(aes(ymax=avg+sd, ymin=avg-sd), position=dodge)
+scale_fill_grey(start=.1,end=0.4)+theme_bw()

I assumed that scale_fill_grey() would be used to change the lightness
or darkness of the grey, but I am wrong.

Any hints how to do this?

Thanks,

Wade

messages.subject: using geom_hline
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I developed a barchart (four bars) showing the probability of a customer
taking a particular service.  The length of each bar is the probability
under a different condition.  The chart is rotated using coord_flip
(bars horizontal) for a better appearance.  I also calculated the take
probability under a base condition that I would like to show as a line
on the same chart.  For this, I used geom_hline(yintercept = base) where
base is the base probability.  The line should be vertical cutting
across all four horizontal bars.  With the bars going horizontally, the
line however only goes as far as the first bar, then stops.  If I don't
flip the bars so that they go vertically, the line goes across the four
bars.  I want the bars to be horizontal and the line to go vertically
across all four bars.  How?  And why does it stop at the first bar when
the bars are horizontal?

Thanks,

Walt

Folks:
Maybe this is a better question for R-Digest but allow me to ask this
here.

What is ggobi and what does it offer? If I understand correctly, it
allows you to dynamically select a set of characteristic values and
look at data based on that. For example,

Product      Customer         Product Group          Sales (this is
weekly sales, longitudinal data)
p1              c1                   pg1                          10
20   40   80  90 ...
p2              c1                   pg1                          16
26   46   88  99 ...
p2              c2                   pg1                          11
12   21   89  90 ...

Now if you want to select p2 and pg1, rows 2 and 3 will be added up
and shown to the user.

I am thinking it is something like the graphing that demand planning
software packages (the ones I know) like i2 DP or SAP APO DP do.

I may be totally wroong. Could you tell me what ggobi does (that
ggplot does not do and the caveat is mentioned in the first few pages
by Hadley in his pdf file that soon to be published).

Thanks.

Satish

messages.subject: Re: ggobi
messages.body_plain:
ggobi does tours and projection pursuit, for example 3D projections (principal coordinates plots of datasets, for example, automatically rotated by projection pursuit and scaled to emphasize contrasts between groups); also dynamic selection of the axes

Suppose that I think STRUCTURE is a piece of garbage and decide that sphered principal coordinates are good enough for me to represent the proportions of genetic ancestry in a large study.  (Wouldn't want to have our conclusions screwed up by "associating" a gene with a disease when that disease and that gene are, by coincidence, unusually well represented in a particular ethnic group or groups)  Ggobi is nice because you can monkey around with the data on the fly to determine which PCs cleanly separate which ethnic groups (e.g. Yorubans vs. everyone else) and additionally label points by their self-reported ethnicity, residence, whatever.  It's a great exploratory tool once you get used to it.

I like to use it for quality control in microarray studies, personally; once a sensible QA pipeline has been established, it's no longer an issue, but when gauging the effectiveness of automated QC or of metrics for the same, it's quite handy.

Try doing some of the examples, particularly with 2D and 2D+1D tours.  That's far better than any explanation I can write.

Hope this helps.

--t

maybe your system is missing some fonts.

When I plot this:

ggplot(mtcars)+geom_point(aes(pmg,cyl))

and export the plot to a pdf file, okular tells me it uses the following
fonts (pdf properties dialog):

 - Helvetica    /usr/share/font/type1/gsfonts/n019003l.pfb
 - ZapfDingbats /usr/share/font/type1/gsfonts/d050000l.pfb

The one responsible for the points should be ZapfDingbats, which are
part of the gsfonts package (in ubuntu).

If it is a font problem, you can also define the fonts yourself with the
parameter font:

  fonts: a character vector specifying R graphics font family names
         for fonts which will be included in the PDF file.  Defaults
         to 'NULL'.

or try this option:

  useDingbats: logical.  Should small circles be rendered _via_ the
         Dingbats font?  Defaults to 'TRUE', which produces smaller
         and better output. Setting this to 'FALSE' can
         work around font display problems in broken PDF viewers. See
         the 'Note' for a possible fix for such viewers.

see ?pdf

regards,
 stefan

messages.subject: Speeding up GGPlot2 plotting...
messages.body_plain:
In the example below it appears that qplot requires the following amount of time on an XP machine with 3.25 GB of RAM and 3.0 GHz Duo:
> ptm_qplot_time
   user  system elapsed
  17.62    1.11   19.34

For the example below is there a way to speed up the amount of time required for ggplot2?

I'm curious about any possible shortcuts for accelerating the amount of time required to produce the plots using ggplot2.

Thank you for any feedback any insight that can be provided.

sample_size<-200
Home_SqFootage<-sample(1200:3600, size=sample_size, rep=T)
Home_Year_Built<-sample(1989:2008, size=sample_size, rep=T)
Home_Year_Sold<-sample(1989:2008, size=sample_size, rep=T)
Home_DF<-data.frame(SqFootage=Home_SqFootage, YearBuilt=as.character(Home_Year_Built), YearSold=as.character(Home_Year_Sold))
label_length<-length(unique(Home_DF$YearBuilt))
all_labels<-sort(unique(Home_DF$YearBuilt))
new_label<-NULL
for(ii in 1:label_length)
{
        if(ii%%2 == 0)
        {
                new_label_tmp<-as.character(all_labels[ii])
        } else {
                new_label_tmp<-c("")
        }

        new_label<-c(new_label, new_label_tmp)
}
ptm_qplot<-proc.time()
qplot(YearBuilt, data = Home_DF, binwidth = 1, fill = factor(Home_DF$SqFootage)) +
                     scale_fill_discrete("Sq Footage") +
                     scale_y_continuous("Counts") +
                     scale_x_discrete("Year Built", labels=new_label)
ptm_qplot_time<-proc.time() - ptm_qplot

messages.body_plain:
Here are some timing results for using qplot and ggplot2.

ptm_qplot_9<-proc.time()
require(nlme, quiet = TRUE, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
model <- lme(height ~ age, data = Oxboys, random = ~ 1 + age | Subject)
oplot <- ggplot(data=Oxboys, aes(x=age, y=height, group=Subject)) + geom_line()
age_grid <- seq(-1, 1, length = 10)
subjects <- unique(Oxboys$Subject)
preds <- expand.grid(age = age_grid, Subject = subjects)
preds$height <- predict(model, preds)
oplot + geom_line(data = preds, colour = "#3366FF", size= 0.4)
ptm_qplot_9_time<-proc.time() - ptm_qplot_9
ptm_qplot_9_time
# Results
# user  system elapsed
#  1.543   0.033   1.640

mpg2 <- subset(mpg, cyl != 5 & drv %in% c("4", "f"))

messages.subject: plyr and plotting datetimes
messages.body_plain:
I am new to R and ggplot (and programming in general) and am trying to
learn the ropes using a simple dataset that tracks the sleeping habits
of my newborn son (it records when he falls asleep and when he wakes
up). The idea is to calculate discrete sleep durations and create
plots based on total hours slept/day, average sleeping time, common
nap times, etc. I've included reference code and an example of the
dataset at the end of the message. I'm currently running R 2.9.2 and
the latest version of ggplot2.

Questions:

1) I've done some data manipulation but it seems to me I should be
able to do the same with less code using plyr. Unfortunately, I must
be missing something basic (I've looked through the documentation) and
can't seem to figure out how to use ddply and summarize to wrap
multiple steps into a single (or fewer) step(s). Can someone point me
in the right direction?

2) I can't seem to figure out how to plot dates/datetimes. I get the
error "Error in units == units[1L] : comparison of these types is not
implemented." I tried using scale_x_datetime(). I get the feeling I
must not be understanding fundamental about handling datetimes.

Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Data:

> head(ethandata)
  action_name action_value action_unit         action_time
1      gnight           NA                                 2009-10-21 01:40:11
2    gmorning           NA                               2009-10-21 01:15:40
3      gnight           NA                                 2009-10-21 00:45:29
4       drank           NA            milk               2009-10-21 00:00:23
5      diaper           NA                                 2009-10-20 22:30:37
6       drank           NA            milk               2009-10-20 22:30:29

> head(naps)
     sleep                  gn                     day
1  30 mins 2009-10-21 00:45:29      2009-10-21
2 120 mins 2009-10-20 19:30:14     2009-10-20
3  26 mins 2009-10-20 17:10:17      2009-10-20
4 156 mins 2009-10-20 12:50:30     2009-10-20
5 217 mins 2009-10-20 08:06:22     2009-10-20
6  98 mins 2009-10-20 06:02:23      2009-10-20

Code:

ethandata <- read.csv("ethan2.txt", sep="\t", stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
ethandata <- transform(ethandata,
                                 day = as.Date(ethandata$action_time,
'%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'),
                                 hour =
as.POSIXct(ethandata$action_time, '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'))

ethan <- subset(ethandata,
                        action_name == "gnight" | action_name == "gmorning",
                        select = c(action_name, day, hour))

ethan.gnight <- subset(ethan, action_name == "gnight",
                                 select = c(action_name, day, hour))
ethan.gmorning <- subset(ethandata, action_name == "gmorning",
                                      select = c(action_name, day, hour))

if(ethan.gnight$hour[1]<ethan.gmorning$hour[1]){
    sleep <- round(ethan.gmorning$hour[1:length(ethan.gnight$hour)] -
ethan.gnight$hour)
} else
    sleep <- round(ethan.gmorning$hour[1:length(ethan.gnight$hour)-1]
- ethan.gnight$hour[-c(1)])

naps <- data.frame(sleep, gn = ethan.gnight$hour[-c(1)], day =
ethan.gnight$day[-c(1)])

qplot(gn, sleep, data=naps, geom="line") + scale_x_datetime()

messages.body_plain:
I have a results table in which each row represents an indicator and
some historical performance data on that indicator, and because of the
way I want to convey the data I'm taking a funky (non-melted) approach
-- essentially hand-rolling the layers to plot specific points,
segments, and lineranges and using facet_grid() on the indicator value
to keep things nice and separate. I'm mostly happy with the results
but my efforts to sort the facets are falling down this time. I've got
the underlying factor reordered by one of the values in the plot; but
no matter what I do with regard to reordering the underlying factor,
it still displays the strips in alpha order. When I inspect the data
slot within the resulting ggplot object, the ordering of the factor is
intact -- but it's not getting implemented in the plot.

Is something about my approach causing ggplot2 to ignore level order?
Or is something else going on here? Any/all insights would be much
appreciated.

If needed I can extract a reproducible example...but I thought I'd
just throw out the question and see if there are some obvious answers
or known conditions that will force ggplot2 to do it's own thing w/
strip order.

I'm still on R 2.90 but latest ggplot2 version.

Thanks,

messages.body_plain:
Welcome to R!

> 1) Beanplots - I'm guessing that it's possible to reproduce these
> plots using ggplot2, but I've no clue as to how.  Has anybody

A what? (google, google) Oh, interesting. Sorta like a violin plot
with really wide rug lines down the middle. There's a beanplot package
for R. No, I don't think anyone's ported it to ggplot2. Depending on
whether the beanplot package separates the computations from the
graphical code, it might not be hard to use its calculations in
combination with stat_summary to generate the plot, at least the
single-variable version.

> 2) 2nd x axis.  I understand and accept the limitation on 2nd axes as
> enforced by ggplot2, but I am curious as to whether the location of
> the x axis can be changed.  I would like to plot how concentrations of
> contaminants changes down a soil profile and it makes more sense (as
> well as commonly accepted) to have an x axis on the top rather than
> the bottom.  Can this be done?

I don't think so.

> 3) Censored data:  How does one deal with this in ggplot2?  I've been
> using the NADA package which does a pretty good job, but I prefer the
> aesthetics of ggplot2.

What would you like ggplot2 to do? The data doesn't know it's
censored, so you have to tell ggplot to do something different. You
could use the subset option to plot the points that are at the
censoring boundaries differently somehow, perhaps using a different
geom.

 -Harlan

messages.subject: Re: facet_grid() ignores underlying factor level order - why?
messages.subject_clean: facet_grid() ignores underlying factor level order - why?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It seems strange because ggplot does take into account the order of
factor levels, not their order of appearance in the data or their
alphanumeric order (as far as I know).
For example:

d <- data.frame(fac=factor(rep(c("a", "b", "c"), 3), levels=c("b",
"c", "a")), x=rnorm(9), y=rnorm(9))
qplot(x,y,data=d, facets=.~fac)

In this example, facets do appear in the order b, c, a.
So I think you should provide a reproducible example to give a clear
view of the problem.

On 26 oct, 00:32, Shelby <shelba...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I have a results table in which each row represents an indicator and
> some historical performance data on that indicator, and because of the
> way I want to convey the data I'm taking a funky (non-melted) approach
> -- essentially hand-rolling the layers to plot specific points,
> segments, and lineranges and using facet_grid() on the indicator value
> to keep things nice and separate. I'm mostly happy with the results
> but my efforts to sort the facets are falling down this time. I've got
> the underlying factor reordered by one of the values in the plot; but
> no matter what I do with regard to reordering the underlying factor,
> it still displays the strips in alpha order. When I inspect the data
> slot within the resulting ggplot object, the ordering of the factor is
> intact -- but it's not getting implemented in the plot.
>
> Is something about my approach causing ggplot2 to ignore level order?
> Or is something else going on here? Any/all insights would be much
> appreciated.
>
> If needed I can extract a reproducible example...but I thought I'd
> just throw out the question and see if there are some obvious answers
> or known conditions that will force ggplot2 to do it's own thing w/
> strip order.
>
> I'm still on R 2.90 but latest ggplot2 version.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Shelby

messages.subject: Re: Using a background image
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I suppose you could define a custom grob to use for the
panel.background object, though I don't know if you gain much in
efficiency,

require(pixmap)
require(RGraphics)

pixmapGrob <-
function (pic, x=0.5, y=0.5, ...)
{
  pic = as(pic, "pixmapIndexed")
  width =  unit(pic@bbox[3], "points")
  height =  unit(pic@bbox[4], "points")
  Z <- pic@index[nrow(pic@index):1, ,
               drop = FALSE]
  vp <-
  viewport(x=x, y=y)
  child <-
  imageGrob(nrow(Z), ncol(Z), col=pic@col[Z], gp=gpar(col=NA),
by=FALSE, vp=vp, ...)

  gTree(width= convertUnit(width, "in", val=TRUE),
        height=convertUnit(height, "in", val=TRUE) ,
        children=gList(child), childrenvp=vp, cl="pixmap")

}

background = function(){
 x <- read.pnm(system.file("pictures/logo.ppm", package="pixmap")[1])
	pixmapGrob(x)
}

d = data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10)

p <- qplot(x,y,data=d) + theme_bw() +
	opts(panel.background = background)

(result attached)

An alternative option could be to use the tikzDevice package, which
might let you insert a picture during the latex processing of the tikz
commands (here latex would definitely be much faster than R for a
large image). The tricky part is positioning (the tikzDevice vignette
has an example of annotations).

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: ensuring dimensions yield circles when using polar coordinates
messages.subject_clean: ensuring dimensions yield circles when using polar coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm using ggplot2 to display a parameter space (values of kappa
specifying a Von Mises distribution) that consists of circles. The
code below yields a 2x5 matrix of circles, or at least it should; I've
attempted to specify the pdf dimensions by hand to make sure the
circles are truly circles and not elliptical, but I'd like to know if
there's any way to have the dimensions set automatically to ensure the
circles are true circles. Any thoughts?

library(CircStats)
library(ggplot2)

kappa = exp(seq(0,4,length.out=10))
x = seq(-180,180,10)

a = ldply(
	kappa
	, .fun = function(kappa){
		d = dvm(x*pi/180,0,kappa)
		d = d-min(d)
		d = d/max(d)
		to_return = data.frame(
			kappa = kappa
			, x = x
			, d = d
		)
		return(to_return)
	}
)
p = ggplot(
	data = a
	, mapping = aes(
		x = x
		, y = factor(1)
		, colour = d
		, fill = d
	)
)+facet_wrap(~kappa,ncol=5,as.table=FALSE)+
geom_bar(
	width=1
	,stat='identity'
)+scale_fill_gradient(
	low = muted('blue')
	, high = muted('red')
	, space = 'Lab'
)+scale_colour_gradient(
	low = muted('blue')
	, high = muted('red')
	, space = 'Lab'
)+scale_y_discrete(
	name=''
	,breaks=100
)+scale_x_continuous(
	name=''
	,breaks=0
)+coord_polar(
	theta='x'
)+opts(
	legend.position='none'
	, panel.grid.major = theme_blank()
	, panel.grid.minor = theme_blank()
	, axis.title.y = theme_blank()
	, axis.text.y = theme_blank()
	, axis.title.x = theme_blank()
	, axis.text.x = theme_blank()
	, axis.ticks = theme_blank()
)
ggsave(p,file='kappa_space.pdf',width = 10,height = 4.5)

--
Mike Lawrence

Dalhousie University

I see the "smaller font" on 1996 and 1998, but I think it's just a
kerning issue (ie 1 is thinner than 2).  If you make the graph thinner
so that they are right next to each other you'll see that the other
three numbers line up right, it's almost as if the number 1 is in the
'right-hand side' of the character position, this is very unlikely to
be something that ggplot2 is causing, most likely a font issue.

Of course the År label looks funny; it has one of those funny circles
on top of the letter!  (Which is to say, not sure that poor english
writers have enough experience with these type of characters to know
what funny means in this context; the capital does look substantially
higher than the smaller case letter, looks like the font doesn't
adjust the height of the capitalized letters when adding diacriticals,
again probably a font issue.  Try a different font?)

This is a good looking graph, btw (although you probably want to drop
the 0.5 legend, move alpha=0.5 outside the call to aes in geom_vline).

--J

by=FALSE, vp=vp, ...)

  gTree(width= convertUnit(width, "in", val=TRUE),
        height=convertUnit(height, "in", val=TRUE),

messages.body_plain:
Yep, that's how it's supposed to work - but it doesn't like some
aspect of what I'm doing. I've tried only plotting individual
components of what I have below in order to isolate the part that's
causing the breakdown, but to no avail.

I'm pasting my code and example data below. If anyone has any
thoughts, I'd be very grateful to hear them!

##==={{{1 PLOT TEMPLATE: SURVEY "ZAG" PLOTS
##==={{{2 Manipulate data to form wrapped labels in desired display
order for plot
zagplotdata <- function(df, labelorder='asis') {
    # create temporary column with wrapped labels for plotting
    wraplength <- max(20,ceiling(max(sapply(as.character(df
$IndicatorName),nchar))/2))
    df$IndicatorShort <- factor(sapply(df$IndicatorName,function(x)
paste(strwrap(x,wraplength),collapse='\n')))
    # order indicator labels by dataset order or by increasing/
decreasing order of Percent_2009 value
    reorderval <- 1:nrow(df)
    if (labelorder == 'increasing') {
        reorderval <- order(df$Percent_2009)
    }
    if (labelorder == 'decreasing') {
        reorderval <- order(-df$Percent_2009)
    }
    df$IndicatorShort <- factor(df$IndicatorShort,levels=df
$IndicatorShort[reorderval],ordered=TRUE)
    # return dataframe for plotting
    df <- df[,c
('IndicatorShort','Percent_2009','Percent_2007','Percent_2008','trendind','change0809ind')]
    return(df)
}

##==={{{2 Color scales for use in plot
trendscale.pos <- c('nodata' = 'darkgrey', 'Not Tested' = 'darkgrey',
'Decreasing(**)' = 'red3', 'Decreasing(*)' = 'darkorange2', 'No Sig
Diff' = 'gold2', 'Increasing(*)' = 'limegreen', 'Increasing(**)' =
'forestgreen')

##==={{{2 Code to generate plot
zagplot <- function(df, titletext = NA, ...) {
    mylimits <- c(min(subset(df,select=c('Percent_2009',
'Percent_2008', 'Percent_2007')),na.rm=TRUE),
                max(subset(df,select=c('Percent_2009', 'Percent_2008',
'Percent_2007')),na.rm=TRUE)+5)
    myplot <- ggplot(data=zagplotdata(df),aes
(x='08/09',y=Percent_2009)) +
    geom_linerange(size=2,aes
(x='08/09',ymin=Percent_2009,ymax=Percent_2008,colour=trendind)) +
    geom_linerange(size=.75,linetype=2,aes
(x='07/08',ymin=Percent_2008,ymax=Percent_2007,colour=trendind)) +
    geom_segment(size=.75,linetype=2,aes
(x='07/08',xend='08/09',y=Percent_2008,yend=Percent_2008,colour=trendind))
+
    geom_point(size=4.5,shape=16,aes
(x='08/09',y=Percent_2009,colour=change0809ind)) +
    geom_point(size=2,shape=18,aes
(x='08/09',y=Percent_2008,colour=trendind)) +
    geom_point(size=3,shape=18,aes
(x='07/08',y=Percent_2007,colour=trendind)) +
    geom_text(aes(x='08/09',label=Percent_2009),size=3,hjust=-.75) +
    scale_colour_manual('Key',value=trendscale.pos) +
    scale_x_discrete('') +
    scale_y_continuous('Percent',limits=mylimits) +
    facet_grid(IndicatorShort~.) +
    coord_flip() +
    opts(strip.text.y=theme_text(angle=0,hjust=.
2,size=8),legend.position='right',legend.text=theme_text
(size=8),axis.text.y=theme_text(size=8),title=titletext)
    return(myplot)
}

##==={{{1 GENERATE ZAG PLOT FOR TEST DATA
testdata <- data.frame(
    Percent_2009 = c(69.6, 26.0, 81.9),
    Percent_2008 = c(71.8, 18.0, 83.3),

Diff'),
        levels=c('Decreasing(**)', 'Decreasing(*)', 'No Sig Diff',
'Increasing(*)', 'Increasing(**)', 'Not Tested')),
    trendind = factor(c('Decreasing(**)', 'Increasing(**)', 'Increasing
(**)'),
        levels = c('Decreasing(**)', 'Decreasing(*)', 'No Sig Diff',
'Increasing(*)', 'Increasing(**)', 'Not Tested')),
    IndicatorName=factor(c('Indicator A', 'Indicator B', 'Indicator
C'),
        levels=c('Indicator A', 'Indicator B', 'Indicator C')))

zagplot(testdata,titletext='My Test Plot') # strips appear in ABC
order
zagplot(testdata,titletext='My Test Plot',labelorder='increasing') #
hmm...strips still appear in ABC order
zagplot(testdata,titletext='My Test Plot',labelorder='decreasing') #

I'm new to ggplot2 and am pleased with what I've been able to do

and annotate() and/or themability for these elements in a future
version.

have been very happy not to dig so deep.

Best,

ronald

messages.subject: Re: Chemical structures in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Interesting idea, I'd be keen to hear about an R package to draw
chemical structures.

One possible hack is to use the tikzDevice package that lets you use
arbitrary LaTeX code in a plot, which is subsequently processed by
LaTeX (similar to psfrag in this regard). I found a small LaTeX
package with chemical macros, and with a little tweaking of the
margins you can get a decent result,

options(tikzLatexPackages =
c(getOption('tikzLatexPackages'),"\\usepackage{acide-amine}\n"))

d = data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10, f=factor(sample(letters[1:2], 10, repl=TRUE)))

p <- qplot(x,y,data=d) + theme_bw() +
  opts(plot.margin = unit(c(1, 1, 5, 1), "lines"),
       axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 12 *
        0.8, lineheight = 0.9, vjust = 10)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 8), labels=c("\\phe{15}", "\\leu{15}"))

tikz("annotation.tex",standAlone=T,width=4,height=4)
print(p)
dev.off()

(output attached)

HTH,

baptiste

Hi Felipe,
I think it's fine to add new lines to the axis label from a ggplot2
perspective. However, I tend to think of captions as not being part of
the graphic, but part of the text in which the graphic appears. Why go
to the trouble of adding a caption to the graphic image when you could
just type it in your LaTeX/Word/html/whatever document?

messages.body_plain:
The easiest way is to compute the densities yourself:

variable <- rep(1:5, each=1000)

x <- rnorm(variable, variable)
dat <- data.frame(variable, x)

xgrid <- seq(min(dat$x), max(dat$x), length = 100)

density <- ddply(dat, "variable", function(df) {
  dens <- with(df, dnorm(xgrid, mean(x), sd(x)))
  data.frame(x = xgrid, dens)
})

ggplot(data=dat, aes(x)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y=..density..), col='grey50', fill="grey") +
  geom_density() +

  geom_line(aes(y = dens), data = density) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales='free')

messages.subject_clean: Multiple plots with same size of y-axis viewport
messages.body_plain:
Below is a minimal example (hopefully it could be simplified a little bit),

p1 <- qplot(1,1000) + ylab("double\nline")
p2 <- qplot(1,1)

g1 <- ggplotGrob(p1)
g2 <- ggplotGrob(p2)

## retrieve the relevant components and
## strip their viewport (needed to calculate the sizes before drawing)
ytit1 <- editGrob(getGrob(g1,"axis.title.y.text",grep=TRUE), vp=NULL)
ylab1 <- editGrob(getGrob(g1,"axis.text.y.text",grep=TRUE), vp=NULL)
ytit2 <- editGrob(getGrob(g2,"axis.title.y.text",grep=TRUE), vp=NULL)
ylab2 <- editGrob(getGrob(g2,"axis.text.y.text",grep=TRUE), vp=NULL)

gl <- grid.layout(nrow=2)
vp <- viewport(layout=gl)
pushViewport(vp)
## calculate the sizes
width2 <- grobWidth(ytit2) + grobWidth(ylab2)
width1 <- grobWidth(ytit1) + grobWidth(ylab1)
width.diff <- width2-width1

pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.row=1))
pushViewport(viewport(x=unit(1, "npc"), width=unit(1, "npc"), just="right"))
grid.draw(g1)
upViewport(2)
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.row=2))
pushViewport(viewport(x=unit(1, "npc"), width=unit(1, "npc")+
width.diff, just="right"))
grid.draw(g2)
upViewport(2)

HTH,

baptiste

A slightly more generic version,

p1 <- qplot(1,1000) + ylab("double\nline")

align.plots <- function(...){

  dots <- list(...)
  dots <- lapply(dots, ggplotGrob)
  ytitles <- lapply(dots, function(.g)
editGrob(getGrob(.g,"axis.title.y.text",grep=TRUE), vp=NULL))
  ylabels <- lapply(dots, function(.g)
editGrob(getGrob(.g,"axis.text.y.text",grep=TRUE), vp=NULL))
  ## one should also deal with the legends...

  gl <- grid.layout(nrow=length(dots))
  vp <- viewport(layout=gl)
  pushViewport(vp)
  widths <- mapply(`+`, e1=lapply(ytitles, grobWidth),
                        e2= lapply(ylabels, grobWidth), SIMPLIFY=F)
  widths.max <- max(do.call(unit.c, widths))

  for(ii in seq_along(dots)){
  pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.row=ii))
  pushViewport(viewport(x=unit(1, "npc"), width=unit(1, "npc") -
widths.max + widths[[ii]], just="right"))
  grid.draw(dots[[ii]])
  upViewport(2)
}
}
